edges.effect_quant: Recent syntheses disagree on how reliable the tear-film benefit is. A 2023 meta-analysis of 19 RCTs involving 4,246 patients found significant improvements in tear break-up time, Schirmer scores, osmolarity, and symptom scores with omega-3 treatment, and an earlier 17-trial meta-analysis reported similar improvement in tear metrics. But an updated 8-RCT meta-analysis found no evident improvement in corneal staining, TBUT, or Schirmer score despite some symptom improvement, leaving the overall clinical signal mixed.
edges.population: adults with dry eye disease using omega-3 fatty acid supplementation as adjunctive therapy
edges.mechanism: Omega-3 fatty acids may alter tear-film lipid composition, reduce ocular-surface inflammation, and improve meibomian-gland function, but response appears to vary by dry-eye subtype, dose, and trial design.
edges.summary: The literature does not support a universally reliable tear-film benefit, but it does support the possibility of benefit in some dry-eye populations. The safest framing is mixed evidence with plausible upside, not established efficacy for everyone.
edges.caveats: Dry eye is heterogeneous, and placebo choice, dose, EPA:DHA composition, treatment duration, and co-treatments all affect results. Symptom improvements do not always line up with objective tear-film metrics across studies.
